Among the 7 actions NIST suggests for Govern 1.4, NIST suggests establishing and regularly reviewing documentation policies addressing information related to AI actor contact information, business justification, scope and usages, expected and potential risks and impacts, assumptions and limitations, description and characterization of training data, algorithmic methodology, evaluated alternative approaches, description of output data, testing and validation results (including explanatory visualizations and information), down- and up-stream dependencies, plans for deployment, monitoring, and change management, and stakeholder engagement plans [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 1]; verifying that documentation policies for AI systems are standardized across the organization and remain current [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 2]; establishing policies for a model documentation inventory system and regularly reviewing its completeness, usability, and efficacy [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 3]; establishing mechanisms to regularly review the efficacy of risk management processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 4]; identifying AI actors responsible for evaluating the efficacy of risk management processes and approaches and for course-correction based on results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 5]; establishing policies and processes regarding public disclosure of the use of AI and risk management material such as impact assessments, audits, model documentation, and validation and testing results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 6]; and documenting and reviewing the use and efficacy of different types of transparency tools and following industry standards at the time a model is in use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.4 Action 7].

Among the 3 actions NIST suggests for Govern 1.1, NIST suggests maintaining awareness of the applicable legal and regulatory considerations and requirements specific to industry, sector, and business purpose, as well as the application context of the deployed AI system [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.1 Action 1]; aligning risk management efforts with applicable legal standards [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.1 Action 2]; and maintaining policies for training (and re-training) organizational staff about necessary legal or regulatory considerations that may impact AI-related design, development, and deployment activities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.1 Action 3].

Among the 15 actions NIST suggests for Govern 1.2, NIST suggests defining key terms and concepts related to AI systems and the scope of their purposes and intended uses [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 1]; connecting AI governance to existing organizational governance and risk controls [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 2]; aligning to broader data governance policies and practices, particularly the use of sensitive or otherwise risky data [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 3]; detailing standards for experimental design, data quality, and model training [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 4]; outlining and documenting risk mapping and measurement processes and standards [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 5]; detailing model testing and validation processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 6]; detailing review processes for legal and risk functions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 7]; establishing the frequency of and detail for monitoring, auditing, and review processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 8]; outlining change management requirements [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 9]; outlining processes for internal and external stakeholder engagement [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 10]; establishing whistleblower policies to facilitate reporting of serious AI system concerns [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 11]; detailing and testing incident response plans [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 12]; verifying that formal AI risk management policies align to existing legal standards and industry best practices and norms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 13]; establishing AI risk management policies that broadly align to AI system trustworthy characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 14]; and verifying that formal AI risk management policies include currently deployed and third-party AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.2 Action 15].

Among the 5 actions NIST suggests for Govern 1.3, NIST suggests establishing policies to define mechanisms for measuring or understanding an AI system's potential impacts, for example via regular impact assessments at key stages in the AI lifecycle, connected to system impacts and frequency of system updates [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 1]; establishing policies to define mechanisms for measuring or understanding the likelihood of an AI system's impacts and their magnitude at key stages in the AI lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 2]; establishing policies that define assessment scales for measuring potential AI system impact, which may be qualitative such as red-amber-green (RAG), or may entail simulations or econometric approaches [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 3]; establishing policies for assigning an overall risk measurement approach for an AI system or its important components, for example via multiplication or combination of a mapped risk's impact and likelihood (risk ≈ impact x likelihood) [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 4]; and establishing policies to assign systems to uniform risk scales that are valid across the organization's AI portfolio (for example, documentation templates), acknowledging that risk tolerance and risk levels may change over the lifecycle of an AI system [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.3 Action 5].

Among the 7 actions NIST suggests for Govern 1.5, NIST suggests establishing policies to allocate appropriate resources and capacity for assessing impacts of AI systems on individuals, communities, and society [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 1]; establishing policies and procedures for monitoring and addressing AI system performance and trustworthiness, including bias and security problems, across the lifecycle of the system [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 2]; establishing policies for AI system incident response, or confirming that existing incident response policies apply to AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 3]; establishing policies to define organizational functions and personnel responsible for AI system monitoring and incident response activities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 4]; establishing mechanisms to enable the sharing of feedback from impacted individuals or communities about negative impacts from AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 5]; establishing mechanisms to provide recourse for impacted individuals or communities to contest problematic AI system outcomes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 6]; and establishing opt-out mechanisms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.5 Action 7].

Among the 6 actions NIST suggests for Govern 2.1, NIST suggests establishing policies that define the AI risk management roles and responsibilities for positions directly and indirectly related to AI systems, including but not limited to boards of directors or advisory committees, senior management, AI audit functions, product management, project management, AI design, AI development, human-AI interaction, AI testing and evaluation, AI acquisition and procurement, impact assessment functions, and oversight functions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 1]; establishing policies that promote regular communication among AI actors participating in AI risk management efforts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 2]; establishing policies that separate management of AI system development functions from AI system testing functions to enable independent course-correction of AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 3]; establishing policies to identify, increase the transparency of, and prevent conflicts of interest in AI risk management efforts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 4]; establishing policies to counteract confirmation bias and market incentives that may hinder AI risk management efforts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 5]; and establishing policies that incentivize AI actors to collaborate with existing legal, oversight, compliance, or enterprise risk functions in their AI risk management activities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.1 Action 6].

Among the 6 actions NIST suggests for Govern 2.2, NIST suggests establishing policies for personnel addressing ongoing education about applicable laws and regulations for AI systems, potential negative impacts that may arise from AI systems, organizational AI policies, and trustworthy AI characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 1]; ensuring that trainings are suitable across AI actor sub-groups, for AI actors carrying out technical tasks (for example, developers and operators) as compared to AI actors in oversight roles (for example, legal, compliance, and audit) [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 2]; ensuring that trainings comprehensively address technical and socio-technical aspects of AI risk management [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 3]; verifying that organizational AI policies include mechanisms for internal AI personnel to acknowledge and commit to their roles and responsibilities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 4]; verifying that organizational policies address change management and include mechanisms to communicate and acknowledge substantial AI system changes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 5]; and defining paths along internal and external chains of accountability to escalate risk concerns [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.2 Action 6].

Among the 2 actions NIST suggests for Govern 2.3, NIST suggests that organizational management declare risk tolerances for developing or using AI systems, support AI risk management efforts and play an active role in such efforts, integrate a risk and harm prevention mindset throughout the AI lifecycle as part of organizational culture, support competent risk management executives, and delegate the power, resources, and authorization to perform risk management to each appropriate level throughout the management chain [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.3 Action 1]; and that organizations establish board committees for AI risk management and oversight functions and integrate those functions within the organization's broader enterprise risk management approaches [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 2.3 Action 2].

Among the 4 actions NIST suggests for Govern 1.6, NIST suggests establishing policies that define the creation and maintenance of AI system inventories [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 1]; establishing policies that define a specific individual or team that is responsible for maintaining the inventory [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 2]; establishing policies that define which models or systems are inventoried, with preference to inventorying all models or systems or, minimally, high risk models or systems, or systems deployed in high-stakes settings [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 3]; and establishing policies that define model or system attributes to be inventoried, for example documentation, links to source code, incident response plans, data dictionaries, and AI actor contact information [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.6 Action 4].

Among the 4 actions NIST suggests for Govern 1.7, NIST suggests establishing policies for decommissioning AI systems that typically address user and community concerns and reputational risks, business continuity and financial risks, up and downstream system dependencies, regulatory requirements (for example, data retention), potential future legal, regulatory, security, or forensic investigations, and migration to the replacement system if appropriate [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 1]; establishing policies that delineate where and for how long decommissioned systems, models, and related artifacts are stored [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 2]; establishing practices to track accountability and consider how decommission and other adaptations or changes in system deployment contribute to downstream impacts for individuals, groups, and communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 3]; and establishing policies that address ancillary data or artifacts that must be preserved for fulsome understanding or execution of the decommissioned AI system, for example predictions, explanations, intermediate input feature representations, and usernames and passwords [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 1.7 Action 4].

Among the 5 actions NIST suggests for Govern 3.1, NIST suggests defining policies and hiring practices at the outset that promote interdisciplinary roles, competencies, skills, and capacity for AI efforts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 1]; defining policies and hiring practices that lead to demographic and domain expertise diversity, empowering staff with necessary resources and support, and facilitating the contribution of staff feedback and concerns without fear of reprisal [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 2]; establishing policies that facilitate inclusivity and the integration of new insights into existing practice [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 3]; seeking external expertise to supplement organizational diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility where internal expertise is lacking [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 4]; and establishing policies that incentivize AI actors to collaborate with existing nondiscrimination, accessibility and accommodation, and human resource functions, employee resource groups (ERGs), and diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility (DEIA) initiatives [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.1 Action 5].

Among the 8 actions NIST suggests for Govern 3.2, NIST suggests establishing policies and procedures that define and differentiate the various human roles and responsibilities when using, interacting with, or monitoring AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 1]; establishing procedures for capturing and tracking risk information related to human-AI configurations and associated outcomes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 2]; establishing policies for the development of proficiency standards for AI actors carrying out system operation tasks and system oversight tasks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 3]; establishing specified risk management training protocols for AI actors carrying out system operation tasks and system oversight tasks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 4]; establishing policies and procedures regarding AI actor roles and responsibilities for human oversight of deployed systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 5]; establishing policies and procedures defining human-AI configurations (configurations where AI systems are explicitly designated and treated as team members in primarily human teams) in relation to organizational risk tolerances, and associated documentation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 6]; establishing policies to enhance the explanation, interpretation, and overall transparency of AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 7]; and establishing policies for managing risks regarding known difficulties in human-AI configurations, human-AI teaming, and AI system user experience and user interactions (UI/UX) [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 3.2 Action 8].

Among the 5 actions NIST suggests for Govern 4.1, NIST suggests establishing policies that require inclusion of oversight functions (legal, compliance, risk management) from the outset of the system design process [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 1]; establishing policies that promote effective challenge of AI system design, implementation, and deployment decisions, via mechanisms such as the three lines of defense, model audits, or red-teaming, to minimize workplace risks such as groupthink [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 2]; establishing policies that incentivize safety-first mindset and general critical thinking and review at an organizational and procedural level [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 3]; establishing whistleblower protections for insiders who report on perceived serious problems with AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 4]; and establishing policies to integrate a harm and risk prevention mindset throughout the AI lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.1 Action 5].

Among the 4 actions NIST suggests for Govern 4.2, NIST suggests establishing impact assessment policies and processes for AI systems used by the organization [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 1]; aligning organizational impact assessment activities with relevant regulatory or legal requirements [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 2]; verifying that impact assessment activities are appropriate to evaluate the potential negative impact of a system and how quickly a system changes, and that assessments are applied on a regular basis [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 3]; and utilizing impact assessments to inform broader evaluations of AI system risk [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.2 Action 4].

Among the 5 actions NIST suggests for Govern 4.3, NIST suggests establishing policies and procedures to facilitate and equip AI system testing [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 1]; establishing organizational commitment to identifying AI system limitations and sharing of insights about limitations within appropriate AI actor groups [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 2]; establishing policies for reporting and documenting incident response [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 3]; establishing policies and processes regarding public disclosure of incidents and information sharing [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 4]; and establishing guidelines for incident handling related to AI system risks and performance [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 4.3 Action 5].

Among the 3 actions NIST suggests for Govern 5.1, NIST suggests establishing AI risk management policies that explicitly address mechanisms for collecting, evaluating, and incorporating stakeholder and user feedback that could include recourse mechanisms for faulty AI system outputs, bug bounties, human-centered design, user-interaction and experience research, and participatory stakeholder engagement with individuals and communities that may experience negative impacts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.1 Action 1]; verifying that stakeholder feedback is considered and addressed, including environmental concerns, and across the entire population of intended users, including historically excluded populations, people with disabilities, older people, and those with limited access to the internet and other basic technologies [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.1 Action 2]; and clarifying the organization's principles as they apply to AI systems, considering those which have been proposed publicly, to inform external stakeholders of the organization's values, and considering publishing or adopting AI principles [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.1 Action 3].

Among the 5 actions NIST suggests for Govern 5.2, NIST suggests explicitly acknowledging that AI systems, and the use of AI, present inherent costs and risks along with potential benefits [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 1]; defining reasonable risk tolerances for AI systems informed by laws, regulation, best practices, or industry standards [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 2]; establishing policies that ensure all relevant AI actors are provided with meaningful opportunities to provide feedback on system design and implementation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 3]; establishing policies that define how to assign AI systems to established risk tolerance levels by combining system impact assessments with the likelihood that an impact occurs, which often entails some combination of econometric evaluations of impacts and impact likelihoods to assess AI system risk, red-amber-green (RAG) scales for impact severity and likelihood to assess AI system risk, policies for allocating risk management resources along established risk tolerance levels with higher-risk systems receiving more risk management resources and oversight, and policies for approval, conditional approval, and disapproval of the design, implementation, and deployment of AI systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 4]; and establishing policies facilitating the early decommissioning of AI systems that surpass an organization's ability to reasonably mitigate risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Govern 5.2 Action 5].

NIST suggests, among its 12 actions for Measure 1.1, establishing approaches for detecting, tracking, and measuring known risks, errors, incidents, or negative impacts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 1]; identifying testing procedures and metrics to demonstrate whether the system is fit for purpose, functioning as claimed, and trustworthy [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 3]; defining acceptable limits for system performance, including course-correction suggestions when the system performs beyond those limits [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 4]; identifying transparency metrics and accountability metrics for AI designers, developers, and deployers [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 7]; documenting metric selection criteria, including considered but unused metrics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 8]; monitoring AI system external inputs, including training data, models and components reused from other contexts, and third-party tools and resources [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 9]; reporting metrics to inform assessments of system generalizability and reliability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 10]; assessing and documenting pre- versus post-deployment system performance, including existing and emergent risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 11]; and documenting risks or trustworthiness characteristics identified in the Map function that will not be measured, including justification for non-measurement [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.1 Action 12].

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 1.2, assessing the external validity of all measurements [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 1]; assessing the effectiveness of existing metrics and controls on a regular basis throughout the AI system lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 2]; documenting reports of errors, incidents, and negative impacts and assessing the sufficiency and efficacy of existing metrics for repairs and upgrades [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 3]; developing new metrics when existing metrics are insufficient or ineffective [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 4]; developing and utilizing metrics to monitor, characterize, and track external inputs, including third-party tools [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 5]; determining the frequency and scope for sharing metrics and related information with stakeholders and impacted communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 6]; utilizing stakeholder feedback processes established in the Map function to capture, act upon, and share feedback from end users and potentially impacted communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 7]; and collecting and reporting software quality metrics such as rates of bug occurrence and severity, time to response, and time to repair [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.2 Action 8].

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 1.3, utilizing separate testing teams to enable independent decisions and course-correction for AI systems, with processes tracked and changes in performance measured and documented [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 2]; planning and evaluating AI system prototypes with end user populations early and continuously in the AI lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 3]; assessing the independence and stature of TEVV and oversight AI actors to ensure they have the required levels of independence and resources to perform assurance, compliance, and feedback tasks effectively [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 4]; evaluating the effectiveness of external stakeholder feedback mechanisms for eliciting, evaluating, and integrating input from diverse groups and for enhancing AI actor visibility and decision making regarding AI system risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 6 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 7]; and identifying and utilizing participatory approaches for assessing impacts that may arise from changes in system deployment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 1.3 Action 8].

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Measure 2.1, leveraging existing industry best practices for transparency and documentation of all possible aspects of measurements, such as data sheets for data sets and model cards [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 1]; regularly assessing the effectiveness of tools used to document measurement approaches, test sets, metrics, processes, and materials used [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 2]; and updating those tools as needed [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.1 Action 3].

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 2.2, following human subjects research requirements, including informed consent and compensation, during dataset collection activities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 1]; analyzing differences between the intended and actual population of users or data subjects [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 2]; utilizing disaggregated evaluation methods, for example by race, age, gender, ethnicity, ability, or region [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 3]; establishing thresholds and alert procedures for dataset representativeness within the context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 4]; following intellectual property and privacy rights related to datasets and their use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 6]; evaluating data representativeness through investigation of known failure modes, assessment of data quality and diverse sourcing, application of public benchmarks, traditional bias testing, chaos engineering, and stakeholder feedback [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 7]; and using informed consent for individuals providing data used in system testing and evaluation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.2 Action 8].

NIST suggests, among its 9 actions for Measure 2.3, conducting regular and sustained engagement with potentially impacted communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 1]; regularly testing and evaluating systems in non-optimized conditions in collaboration with AI actors in user interaction and user experience roles [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 3]; measuring AI systems prior to deployment in conditions similar to expected scenarios [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 6]; measuring and documenting performance criteria such as validity (false positive rate, false negative rate) and efficiency (training times, prediction latency) related to ground truth within the deployment context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 7]; measuring assurance criteria such as AI actor competency and experience [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 8]; and documenting differences between the measurement setting and the deployment environment(s) [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.3 Action 9].

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Measure 2.4, monitoring and documenting how metrics and performance indicators observed in production differ from those collected during pre-deployment testing, considering error propagation and feedback loop risks when differences are observed [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 1]; monitoring for anomalies using approaches such as control limits, confidence intervals, integrity constraints, and ML algorithms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 3]; verifying that alerts are in place for when distributions in new input data or generated predictions differ from pre-deployment test outcomes, or when anomalies are detected [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 4]; assessing the accuracy and quality of generated outputs against newly collected ground-truth information as it becomes available [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 5]; and utilizing human review to track processing of unexpected data and reliability of generated outputs, warning system users when outputs may be unreliable, and verifying that human overseers have clearly defined responsibilities and training [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.4 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 15 actions for Measure 2.5, establishing or identifying and documenting approaches to measure forms of validity, including construct, internal, and external validity [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 3]; assessing and documenting system variance using standard approaches such as confidence intervals, standard deviation, standard error, bootstrapping, or cross-validation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 4]; establishing or identifying and documenting robustness measures and reliability measures [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 6]; monitoring operating conditions for system performance outside of defined limits [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 11]; defining post-alert actions, such as alerting relevant AI actors, requesting human review, alerting downstream users and stakeholders, tracking and mitigating error propagation, and action logging [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 13]; logging input data and relevant system configuration information whenever there is an attempt to use the system beyond its well-defined range of system validity [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 14]; and modifying the system over time to extend its range of system validity to new operating conditions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.5 Action 15].

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Measure 2.6, thoroughly measuring system performance in development and deployment contexts and under stress conditions, including stress-testing under likely scenarios such as concept drift and high load, testing under conditions similar to past known incidents or near-misses, applying chaos engineering approaches, and documenting the range of conditions under which the system has been demonstrated to fail safely [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 1]; measuring and monitoring system performance in real-time to enable rapid response when AI system incidents are detected [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 2]; collecting pertinent safety statistics such as out-of-range performance, incident response times, and system down time [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 3]; documenting, practicing, and measuring incident response plans for AI system incidents, including measuring response and down times [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 5]; and comparing documented safety testing and monitoring information with established risk tolerances on an ongoing basis [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.6 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 10 actions for Measure 2.7, establishing and tracking AI system security tests and metrics, such as red-teaming activities, frequency and rate of anomalous events, system down-time, incident response times, and time-to-bypass [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 1]; using red-team exercises to actively test the system under adversarial or stress conditions and to evaluate potential mismatches between claimed and actual system performance [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 4]; documenting red-team exercise results as part of continuous improvement efforts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 3]; using countermeasures such as authentication, throttling, differential privacy, and robust ML approaches to increase the range of security conditions under which the system can return to normal function [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 5]; verifying that third-party AI resources and personnel undergo security audits and screenings [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 9]; and utilizing watermarking technologies as a deterrent to data and model extraction attacks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.7 Action 10].

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 2.8, instrumenting the system for measurement and tracking, for example by maintaining histories, audit logs, and other information usable by AI actors to review and evaluate possible sources of error, bias, or vulnerability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 1]; testing provided explanations for calibration with different audiences, including operators, end users, decision makers, and decision subjects, to enable recourse for consequential system decisions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 3]; measuring and documenting human oversight of AI systems, including the degree of oversight provided, statistics about downstream actions such as system overrides, and statistics about reported errors or complaints, time to respond, and response types [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 4]; tracking, documenting, and measuring organizational accountability via policy exceptions and escalations and documenting "go" and "no/go" decisions made by accountable parties [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 5]; and tracking and auditing the effectiveness of organizational mechanisms related to AI risk management, including lines of communication, roles and responsibilities, and organizational accountability roles [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.8 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 11 actions for Measure 2.9, verifying that systems are developed to produce explainable models, post-hoc explanations, and audit logs [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 1]; documenting AI model details including model type, data features, training algorithms, proposed uses, decision thresholds, training data, evaluation data, and ethical considerations [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 4]; establishing, documenting, and reporting performance and error metrics across demographic groups and other segments relevant to the deployment context [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 5]; explaining systems using a variety of methods and testing explanations according to properties such as fidelity, consistency, robustness, and interpretability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 6]; assessing the characteristics of system explanations according to properties such as fidelity, ambiguity, interpretability, interactivity, consistency, and resilience to attack or manipulation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 7]; testing the quality of system explanations with end users and other groups [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 8]; and using transparency tools such as data statements and model cards to document explanatory and validation information [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.9 Action 11].

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Measure 2.10, documenting the collection, use, management, and disclosure of personally sensitive information in datasets in accordance with privacy and data governance policies [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 2]; quantifying privacy-level data aspects such as the ability to identify individuals or groups, for example using k-anonymity metrics, l-diversity, and t-closeness [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 3]; establishing and documenting protocols (authorization, duration, type) and access controls for training sets or production data containing personally sensitive information [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 4]; monitoring internal queries to production data for detecting patterns that isolate personal records [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 5]; and using privacy-enhancing techniques such as differential privacy when publicly sharing dataset information [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.10 Action 7].

NIST suggests, among its 24 actions for Measure 2.11, conducting fairness assessments that identify types of harms, identify across, within, and intersecting groups that might be harmed, quantify harms using general and context-specific fairness metrics, and analyze quantified harms for contextually significant differences [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 1]; using context-specific fairness metrics to examine how system performance varies across groups, within groups, and for intersecting groups [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 7]; defining acceptable levels of difference in performance in accordance with established organizational governance policies, business requirements, regulatory compliance, legal frameworks, and ethical standards within the context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 9]; defining the actions to be taken if disparity levels rise above acceptable levels [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 10]; monitoring system outputs for performance or bias issues that exceed established tolerance levels [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 13]; and evaluating practices along the lifecycle to identify potential sources of human-cognitive bias such as availability, observational, and confirmation bias [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.11 Action 22].

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 2.12, identifying and implementing key indicators of AI system energy and water consumption, efficiency, and/or GHG emissions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 2]; establishing measurable baselines for sustainable AI system operation in accordance with organizational policies, regulatory compliance, legal frameworks, and environmental protection and sustainability norms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 3]; identifying and establishing acceptable resource consumption, efficiency, and GHG emissions levels, along with actions to be taken if indicators rise above acceptable levels [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 5]; and estimating AI system emissions levels throughout the AI lifecycle via carbon calculators or a similar process [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.12 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Measure 2.13, reviewing selected system metrics and associated TEVV processes to determine if they are able to sustain system improvements, including the identification and removal of errors [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 1]; regularly evaluating system metrics for utility and considering descriptive approaches in place of overly complex methods [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 2]; reviewing selected system metrics for acceptability within the end user and impacted community of interest [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 3]; and assessing the effectiveness of metrics for identifying and measuring risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 2.13 Action 4].

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 3.1, comparing AI system risks with simpler or traditional models, human baseline performance, and other manual performance benchmarks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 1]; comparing end user and community feedback about deployed AI systems to internal measures of system performance [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 2]; assessing the effectiveness of metrics for identifying and measuring emergent risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 3]; measuring error response times and tracking response quality [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 4]; and eliciting and tracking feedback from AI actors in user support, incident response, and support roles about the type of metrics, explanations, and other system information required for fulsome resolution of system issues, and about the adequacy of staffing and resources to perform their duties effectively and in a timely manner [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.1 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Measure 3.2, establishing processes for tracking emergent risks that may not be measurable with current approaches, including recourse mechanisms for faulty AI system outputs, bug bounties, human-centered design approaches, user-interaction and experience research, and participatory stakeholder engagement with affected or potentially impacted individuals and communities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 1]; identifying AI actors responsible for tracking emergent risks and inventorying methods [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 2]; and determining and documenting the rate of occurrence and severity level for complex or difficult-to-measure risks when prioritizing new measurement approaches, allocating AI system risk management resources, evaluating AI system improvements, and making go/no-go decisions for subsequent system iterations [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.2 Action 3].

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 3.3, measuring the efficacy of end user and operator error reporting processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 1]; categorizing and analyzing the type and rate of end user appeal requests and results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 2]; measuring feedback activity participation rates and awareness of feedback activity availability [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 3]; utilizing feedback to analyze measurement approaches and determine subsequent courses of action [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 4]; evaluating measurement approaches to determine efficacy for enhancing organizational understanding of real-world impacts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 5]; and analyzing end user and community feedback in close collaboration with domain experts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 3.3 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.1, supporting mechanisms for capturing feedback from system end users, including domain experts, operators, and practitioners, conducted in settings where end users can openly share their doubts and insights about AI system output in connection to their specific context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 1]; identifying and documenting approaches for evaluating and integrating elicited feedback from system end users, in collaboration with human-factors and socio-technical domain experts, to actively inform a process of continual improvement [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 2]; utilizing end user feedback to investigate how selected metrics and measurement approaches interact with organizational and operational contexts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 4]; and identifying and implementing approaches to measure effectiveness and satisfaction with end user elicitation techniques, and documenting results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.1 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.2, integrating feedback from end users, operators, and affected individuals and communities from the Map function as inputs to assess AI system trustworthiness characteristics, ensuring both positive and negative feedback is assessed [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 1]; evaluating feedback regarding end user satisfaction with, and confidence in, AI system performance, including whether output is considered valid, reliable, explainable, and interpretable [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 3]; measuring the frequency of AI systems' override decisions, evaluating and documenting results, and feeding insights back into continual improvement processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 5]; and consulting AI actors in impact assessment, human factors, and socio-technical tasks to assist with analysis and interpretation of results [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.2 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Measure 4.3, developing baseline quantitative measures for trustworthy characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 1]; delimiting and characterizing baseline operation values and states [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 2]; utilizing qualitative approaches to augment and complement quantitative baseline measures, in close coordination with impact assessment, human factors, and socio-technical AI actors [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 3]; monitoring and assessing measurements as part of continual improvement to identify potential system adjustments or modifications [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 4]; performing and documenting sensitivity analysis to characterize actual and expected variance in performance after applying system or procedural updates [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 5]; and documenting decisions related to the sensitivity analysis and recording the expected influence on system performance and identified risks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Measure 4.3 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Manage 1.1, considering trustworthiness characteristics when evaluating AI systems' negative risks and benefits [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.1 Action 1], utilizing TEVV outputs from the MAP and MEASURE functions when considering risk treatment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.1 Action 2], regularly tracking and monitoring negative risks and benefits throughout the AI system lifecycle, including in post-deployment monitoring [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.1 Action 3], regularly assessing and documenting system performance relative to trustworthiness characteristics and tradeoffs between negative risks and opportunities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.1 Action 4], and evaluating tradeoffs in connection with real-world use cases and impacts as enumerated in MAP function outcomes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.1 Action 5].

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Manage 1.2, assigning risk management resources relative to established risk tolerance, such that AI systems with lower risk tolerances receive greater oversight, mitigation, and management resources [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.2 Action 1], documenting AI risk tolerance determination practices and resource decisions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.2 Action 2], and regularly reviewing risk tolerances and re-calibrating, as needed, in accordance with information from AI system monitoring and assessment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.2 Action 3].

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Manage 1.3, observing regulatory and established organizational, sector, discipline, or professional standards and requirements for applying risk tolerances within the organization [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.3 Action 1], documenting procedures for acting on AI system risks related to trustworthiness characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.3 Action 2], prioritizing risks involving physical safety, legal liabilities, regulatory compliance, and negative impacts on individuals, groups, or society [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.3 Action 3], identifying risk response plans and resources and organizational teams for carrying out response functions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.3 Action 4], and storing risk management and system documentation in an organized, secure repository that is accessible by relevant AI actors and appropriate personnel [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.3 Action 5].

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Manage 1.4, documenting residual risks within risk response plans, denoting risks that have been accepted, transferred, or subject to minimal mitigation [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.4 Action 1], establishing procedures for disclosing residual risks to relevant downstream AI actors [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.4 Action 2], and informing relevant downstream AI actors of requirements for safe operation, known limitations, and suggested warning labels as identified in MAP 3.4 [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 1.4 Action 3].

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Manage 2.1, planning and implementing risk management practices in accordance with established organizational risk tolerances [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 1], verifying risk management teams are resourced to carry out functions, including establishing processes for considering methods that are not automated, semi-automated, or other procedural alternatives for AI functions, enhancing AI system transparency mechanisms for AI teams, enabling exploration of AI system limitations by AI teams, and identifying, assessing, and cataloging past failed designs and negative impacts or outcomes to avoid known failure modes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 2], identifying resource allocation approaches for managing risks in systems deemed high-risk, that self-update (adaptive, online, reinforcement self-supervised learning or similar), that are trained without access to ground truth (unsupervised, semi-supervised learning or similar), or with high uncertainty or where risk management is insufficient [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 3], regularly seeking and integrating external expertise and perspectives to supplement organizational diversity (e.g., demographic, disciplinary), equity, inclusion, and accessibility where internal capacity is lacking [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 4], enabling and encouraging regular, open communication and feedback among AI actors and internal or external stakeholders related to system design or deployment decisions [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 5], and preparing and documenting plans for continuous monitoring and feedback mechanisms [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.1 Action 6].

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Manage 2.2, establishing risk controls considering trustworthiness characteristics, including data management, quality, and privacy controls (e.g., minimization, rectification or deletion requests) as part of organizational data governance policies; machine learning and end-point security countermeasures (e.g., robust models, differential privacy, authentication, throttling); business rules that augment, limit, or restrict AI system outputs within certain contexts; utilizing domain expertise related to deployment context for continuous improvement and TEVV across the AI lifecycle; development and regular tracking of human-AI teaming configurations; model assessment and test, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) protocols; use of standardized documentation and transparency mechanisms; software quality assurance practices across the AI lifecycle; and mechanisms to explore system limitations and avoid past failed designs or deployments [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.2 Action 1], establishing mechanisms to capture feedback from system end users and potentially impacted groups while the system is in deployment, including feedback about how changes in system deployment (e.g., introducing new technology, decommissioning algorithms and models, adapting system, model or algorithm) may create negative impacts that are not visible along the AI lifecycle [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.2 Action 2], reviewing insurance policies, warranties, or contracts for legal or oversight requirements for risk transfer procedures [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.2 Action 3], and documenting risk tolerance decisions and risk acceptance procedures [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.2 Action 4].

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Manage 2.3, having protocols, resources, and metrics in place for continual monitoring of AI systems' performance, trustworthiness, and alignment with contextual norms and values [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 1], establishing and regularly reviewing treatment and response plans for incidents, negative impacts, or outcomes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 2], establishing and maintaining procedures to regularly monitor system components for drift, decontextualization, or other AI system behavior factors [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 3], establishing and maintaining procedures for capturing feedback about negative impacts [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 4], verifying contingency processes to handle any negative impacts associated with mission-critical AI systems, and to deactivate systems [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 5], enabling preventive and post-hoc exploration of AI system limitations by relevant AI actor groups [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 6], and decommissioning systems that exceed risk tolerances [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.3 Action 7].

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Manage 2.4, regularly reviewing established procedures for AI system bypass actions, including plans for redundant or backup systems to ensure continuity of operational and/or business functionality [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 1], regularly reviewing system incident thresholds for activating bypass or deactivation responses [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 2], applying change management processes to understand the upstream and downstream consequences of bypassing or deactivating an AI system or AI system components [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 3], applying protocols, resources, and metrics for decisions to supersede, bypass, or deactivate AI systems or AI system components [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 4], preserving materials for forensic, regulatory, and legal review [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 5], conducting internal root cause analysis and process reviews of bypass or deactivation events [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 6], decommissioning and preserving system components that cannot be updated to meet criteria for redeployment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 7], and establishing criteria for redeploying updated system components, in consideration of trustworthiness characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 2.4 Action 8].

NIST suggests, among its 9 actions for Manage 4.1, establishing and maintaining procedures to monitor AI system performance for risks and negative and positive impacts associated with trustworthiness characteristics [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 1], performing post-deployment TEVV tasks to evaluate AI system validity and reliability, bias and fairness, privacy, and security and resilience [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 2], evaluating AI system trustworthiness in conditions similar to the deployment context of use, and prior to deployment [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 3], establishing and implementing red-teaming exercises at a prescribed cadence, and evaluating their efficacy [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 4], establishing procedures for tracking dataset modifications such as data deletion or rectification requests [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 5], establishing mechanisms for regular communication and feedback between relevant AI actors and internal or external stakeholders to capture information about system performance, trustworthiness, and impact [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 6], sharing information about errors, near-misses, and attack patterns with incident databases, other organizations with similar systems, and system users and stakeholders [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 7], responding to and documenting detected or reported negative impacts or issues in AI system performance and trustworthiness [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 8], and decommissioning systems that exceed established risk tolerances [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.1 Action 9].

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Manage 4.2, integrating trustworthiness characteristics into protocols and metrics used for continual improvement [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.2 Action 1], establishing processes for evaluating and integrating feedback into AI system improvements [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.2 Action 2], assessing and evaluating alignment of proposed improvements with relevant regulatory and legal frameworks [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.2 Action 3], assessing and evaluating alignment of proposed improvements connected to the values and norms within the context of use [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.2 Action 4], and documenting the basis for decisions made relative to tradeoffs between trustworthiness characteristics, system risks, and system opportunities [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.2 Action 5].

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Manage 4.3, establishing procedures to regularly share information about errors, incidents, and negative impacts with relevant stakeholders, operators, practitioners, and users, and impacted parties [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.3 Action 1], maintaining a database of reported errors, near-misses, incidents, and negative impacts including date reported, number of reports, assessment of impact and severity, and responses [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.3 Action 2], maintaining a database of system changes, reason for change, and details of how the change was made, tested, and deployed [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.3 Action 3], maintaining version history information and metadata to enable continuous improvement processes [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.3 Action 4], and verifying that relevant AI actors responsible for identifying complex or emergent risks are properly resourced and empowered [NIST AI RMF Playbook Manage 4.3 Action 5].

NIST suggests, among its 13 actions for Map 1.1, maintaining awareness of industry, technical, and applicable legal standards; examining the trustworthiness of the AI system design and considering non-AI solutions; identifying whether non-AI or non-technology alternatives would lead to more trustworthy outcomes; determining and delineating the expected and acceptable AI system context of use, including social norms, impacted individuals, groups, and communities, potential positive and negative impacts, and the operational environment; performing context analysis related to time frame, safety concerns, geographic area, physical environment, ecosystems, social environment, and cultural norms within the intended setting; identifying human-AI interaction and roles, such as whether the application will support or replace human decision making; and planning for risks related to human-AI configurations by documenting requirements, roles, and responsibilities for human oversight of deployed systems. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 9 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 10 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 12 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.1 Action 13]

NIST suggests, among its 2 actions for Map 1.2, establishing interdisciplinary teams that reflect a wide range of skills, competencies, and capabilities, verifying that team membership includes demographic diversity, broad domain expertise, and lived experiences, and documenting team composition; and creating and empowering interdisciplinary expert teams to capture and engage the interdependencies of deployed AI systems and related concepts from disciplines outside of AI practice such as law, sociology, psychology, anthropology, public policy, systems design, and engineering. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.2 Action 2]

NIST suggests, among its 5 actions for Map 1.3, reviewing the documented system purpose from a socio-technical perspective and in consideration of societal values; determining possible misalignment between societal values and stated organizational principles and code of ethics; flagging latent incentives that may contribute to negative impacts; and evaluating AI system purpose in consideration of potential risks, societal values, and stated organizational principles. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.3 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.3 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.3 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.3 Action 5]

NIST suggests, among its 3 actions for Map 1.4, documenting the business value or context of business use; reconciling documented concerns about the system's purpose within the business context of use against the organization's stated values, mission statements, social responsibility commitments, and AI principles; and reconsidering the design, implementation strategy, or deployment of AI systems whose potential impacts do not reflect institutional values. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.4 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.4 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.4 Action 3]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Map 1.5, utilizing existing regulations and guidelines for risk criteria, tolerance, and response; establishing risk tolerance levels for AI systems and allocating appropriate oversight resources to each level; establishing risk criteria in consideration of different sources of risk (e.g., financial, operational, safety and wellbeing, business, reputational, and model risks) and different levels of risk (e.g., from negligible to critical); identifying the maximum allowable risk tolerance above which the system will not be deployed or will need to be prematurely decommissioned; articulating and analyzing tradeoffs across trustworthiness characteristics and documenting them with traceable actions; and reviewing uses of AI systems for "off-label" purposes, especially in settings deemed high-risk. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 2 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.5 Action 6]

NIST suggests, among its 8 actions for Map 1.6, proactively incorporating trustworthy characteristics into system requirements; including potentially impacted groups, communities, and external entities (e.g., civil society organizations, research institutes, local community groups, and trade associations) in the formulation of priorities, definitions, and outcomes during impact assessment activities; conducting qualitative interviews with end users to regularly evaluate expectations and design plans related to human-AI configurations and tasks; and conducting user research to understand the individuals, groups, and communities that will be impacted by the AI, their values and context, and the role of systemic and historical biases, integrating learnings into decisions about data selection and representation. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.6 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.6 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.6 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 1.6 Action 8]

NIST suggests, among its 1 action for Map 2.1, defining and documenting the AI system's existing and potential learning tasks along with known assumptions and limitations. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.1 Action 1]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Map 2.2, documenting settings, environments, and conditions that are outside the AI system's intended use; planning and testing human-AI configurations under close to real-world conditions and documenting the results; documenting dependencies on upstream data and other AI systems, including whether the specified system is an upstream dependency for another AI system or other data; and documenting connections the AI system or data will have to external networks (including the internet), financial markets, and critical infrastructure that have potential for negative externalities. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.2 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.2 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.2 Action 6]

NIST suggests, among its 16 actions for Map 2.3, documenting assumptions made and techniques used in data selection, curation, preparation, and analysis, including identification of constructs and proxy targets and development of indices that operationalize inherently unobservable concepts; documenting known limitations, risk mitigation efforts associated with, and methods used for, training data collection, selection, labeling, cleaning, and analysis; establishing and documenting practices to check for capabilities in excess of those planned for, such as emergent properties, and to revisit prior risk management steps in light of any new capabilities; and establishing processes to test and verify that design assumptions about the set of deployment contexts continue to be accurate and sufficiently complete. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.3 Action 8 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.3 Action 12 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.3 Action 13 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 2.3 Action 14]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Map 3.1, considering performance against human baseline metrics or other standard benchmarks, and incorporating feedback from end users and potentially impacted individuals and communities about perceived system benefits. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.1 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.1 Action 6]

NIST suggests, among its 2 actions for Map 3.2, performing context analysis to map potential negative impacts arising from not integrating trustworthiness characteristics — engaging, where negative impacts are not direct or obvious, with stakeholders external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system and with potentially impacted communities to examine and document who could be harmed, what could be harmed, when harm could arise, and how harm could arise — and identifying and implementing procedures for regularly evaluating the qualitative and quantitative costs of internal and external AI system failures to inform go/no-go deployment decisions throughout the AI system lifecycle. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.2 Action 2]

NIST suggests, among its 2 actions for Map 3.3, considering narrowing contexts for system deployment, including factors related to how outcomes may directly or indirectly affect users, groups, communities, and the environment, the length of time the system is deployed in between re-trainings, the geographical regions in which the system operates, dynamics related to community standards or likelihood of system misuse or abuses, and how AI system features and capabilities can be utilized within other applications or in place of other existing processes; and engaging AI actors from legal and procurement functions when specifying target application scope. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.3 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.3 Action 2]

NIST suggests, among its 10 actions for Map 3.4, defining and developing training materials for proposed end users, practitioners, and operators about AI system use and known limitations; defining and developing certification procedures for operating AI systems within defined contexts of use, including information about what exceeds operational boundaries; and verifying that AI system output is interpretable and unambiguous for downstream decision-making tasks. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.4 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.4 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.4 Action 7]

NIST suggests, among its 6 actions for Map 3.5, identifying and documenting AI systems' features and capabilities that require human oversight in relation to operational and societal contexts, trustworthy characteristics, and risks identified in the Map function; defining and developing training materials for relevant AI actors about AI system performance, context of use, known limitations and negative impacts, and suggested warning labels; and evaluating AI system oversight practices for validity and reliability, retesting and course correcting when oversight practices undergo extensive updates or adaptations. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.5 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.5 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 3.5 Action 5]

NIST suggests, among its 4 actions for Map 5.1, establishing assessment scales for measuring AI systems' impact — which may be qualitative, such as red-amber-green (RAG), or may entail simulations or econometric approaches — documented and applied uniformly across the organization's AI portfolio; identifying and documenting the likelihood and magnitude of system benefits and negative impacts in relation to trustworthiness characteristics; and establishing processes for red teaming to identify and connect system limitations to AI lifecycle stage(s) and potential downstream impacts. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.1 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.1 Action 3 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.1 Action 4]

NIST suggests, among its 7 actions for Map 5.2, establishing and documenting stakeholder engagement processes at the earliest stages of system formulation to identify potential impacts from the AI system on individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society; incorporating quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods in the assessment and documentation of potential impacts; identifying a team, internal or external, that is independent of AI design and development functions to assess AI system benefits and positive and negative impacts and their likelihood and magnitude; and evaluating and documenting stakeholder feedback to assess potential impacts for actionable insights regarding trustworthiness characteristics and changes in design approaches and principles. [NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.2 Action 1 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.2 Action 4 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.2 Action 5 | NIST AI RMF Playbook Map 5.2 Action 6]
